video_title: It's a Bubble. So Why Is Citi's Dirk Willer Buying?
gist: Citi macro strategist Dirk Willer argues US equities have been in a price-defined bubble since mid-2025 but that bubbles should be ridden, not shorted, until liquidity or compute overcapacity ends them; he is cautious on bonds until the Fed is near its last hike, dollar-bullish, and constructive on Brazil and AI-linked Asia, with a post-bubble Fed pivot to zero and gold as the big tail.

themes.theme: Defining and trading the AI bubble

insights.claim: Citi's quant team defines a bubble as a real price move of more than two standard deviations above long-term trend (a definition borrowed from GMO); by this price-based test the US market entered bubble territory around mid-2025.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: A price-based definition is testable and ignores arguments over whether earnings or valuations justify the move.
insights.quote: if someone if something goes up more than two standard deviations against the long-term trend in real terms we call it a bubble

insights.claim: The price-based definition also captures earnings bubbles: scarcity leads buyers to over-order, and analysts project earnings off those inflated bookings, so some high-flyer gross margins are not sustainable.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Reported AI-supply-chain earnings may overstate durable profitability.

insights.claim: Calling it a bubble is not a reason to be bearish: on average the money made inside a bubble is partly given back, so the prescription is to stay invested but avoid leverage and keep hedges on.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Positioning is long-but-hedged rather than short; the debate is about exit timing.
insights.quote: the difference is that you give back a fair chunk of the money that you make while you're in a bubble

insights.claim: Bubble durations vary from many years to abrupt endings like 1929, so the ideal trade is to key off fundamentals: equities typically peak six to nine months before fundamentals (here, compute overcapacity) peak.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Watch for signs of compute overcapacity as the lead indicator for an equity top.

insights.claim: Willer believes compute will eventually be overbuilt because humans over-capitalize an opportunity in proportion to its size, even though Citi's fundamental analysts say overcapacity is not close.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Internal Citi disagreement frames the timing risk: the bubble can run while the end state is still overbuild.

insights.claim: Liquidity withdrawal is usually what pops bubbles: in 2000 the Fed hiked 175bp and injected Y2K liquidity in Q4 1999 (Nasdaq +50% that quarter) then withdrew it in Q1, helping the March peak.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Track Fed liquidity and tightening as the trigger rather than valuation.

insights.claim: The first Fed hike is usually not a problem and the last one is; the first and last coincided only in 1997, so the Fed is unlikely to be far enough along to damage the bubble now.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Tightening is not yet an equity-ending threat.
insights.quote: The first Fed hike is usually not a problem. The last Fed hike is a problem.

insights.claim: Sentiment is unusually subdued for a bubble: the AAII survey is quite bearish, whereas bubbles normally end with retail all in (as seen recently in Korea), which suggests the bubble is not yet at its peak.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Lack of retail euphoria supports staying long.

insights.claim: Bubble markets are narrow by nature, as everyone chases the same shiny thing; outperformance of tech ends when the bubble peaks, and the large sector rotation (utilities, housing, staples, financials) only happens afterward, as in 2000.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Narrow breadth is a feature, not a sell signal; if you dislike tech, the alternatives are bonds and staples.

insights.claim: Citi's Generals indicator takes the top seven S&P names each January 1 and, once the bubble indicator is on, exits when four of the seven break down; this gets out faster than waiting for the S&P to break its 200-day average.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: A concrete rule for exiting a concentrated bubble earlier than fundamentals would signal.

insights.claim: Citi's PULSE indicator (positioning, over-optimism, leverage) is a tactical gauge that calls roughly 5% pullbacks on average and has worked well out of sample.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: A rare indicator after which the S&P reliably falls, useful for tactical hedging.

themes.theme: Seasonality, midterms and rates vs equities

insights.claim: November and December are seasonally strong and stronger still in good years, because investors who feel good about the year preposition for another good one; October strength tends to bring a roughly 5% pullback into the midterms that is quickly recovered afterward.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Year-end rally is the base case, with a possible dip into the midterms as a buying opportunity.

insights.claim: Citi does not expect much market relevance from the midterms, including a Democratic House win as prediction markets forecast; the main risk to a year-end rally is a renewed escalation of the Iran war after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Geopolitics, not US politics, is the key risk to year-end positioning.

insights.claim: The level of interest rates barely matters for equities; what matters is the volatility of the bond selloff, i.e. the MOVE index, and the S&P has so far shrugged off a recent MOVE rise.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Watch MOVE, not the 10-year yield level, as the equity risk trigger.

themes.theme: Reading the Warsh Fed and positioning in bonds

insights.claim: Citi built a Warsh shadow rate by z-scoring every indicator Warsh said he cares about; it tracked Fed funds in the Greenspan 1990s, has been a leading indicator since, and is now at its highs, which Citi reads as a hawkish bias.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: A quantified reaction-function proxy for a chair who gave no explicit guidance.

insights.claim: The early assumption that Warsh would be dovish because of presidential politics fell away, and Citi believes he has enough sway over the committee, citing a unanimous last meeting, although the Fed would not hike if data argued against it.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: The market should price a hawkish bias, not a politically dovish chair.

insights.claim: The S&P usually pulls back a little around the first hike and then ignores policy until the last hike, and Citi argues the Fed is not near overtightening.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Hikes alone are not a reason to leave equities.

insights.claim: The bond rule of thumb is to sell about six months before the first hike and buy back when one hike is left; because the market keeps adding hikes until the Fed sounds close to done, Citi stays cautious and wants the Fed further along before buying duration.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Do not buy bonds against a rolling hike repricing; the 1999 analogy says it is too early.

insights.claim: Decomposing the back-end selloff, nearly all the move is real rates; breakevens (no Fed credibility problem) and asset swap spreads (no fiscal supply problem) did not move, so the market is pricing strong growth, which is why equities can coexist with higher yields.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: The 'bond vigilante' narrative is not what the data show.

insights.claim: The Treasury still has ammunition at the November refunding: it can cut coupon issuance and lean on bills, which the Fed would ultimately absorb via repo pressure, and a TGA drawdown would lower reserves-draining risk; the earlier buyback intervention was a peashooter at the wrong moment, with no panic in the market.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Be cautious on long bonds going into the November refunding; a bill-heavy shift could stabilize the back end like the 2023 buyer strike response.

insights.claim: With 30-year real yields around 3.3%, long-horizon investors may find bonds interesting, since the S&P may not beat 3.3% real if the bubble bursts within about five years, though valuation says nothing over a one-year horizon.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Long-duration bonds are a patient trade, not a near-term one.

insights.claim: Equity market cap was just over 100% of GDP in 2000 and is about 240% now, so a bubble burst would likely produce a bigger recession than the shallow 2001 one; the Fed would cut aggressively, rates could return to zero, and the Fed would probably buy the back end.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Wealth-effect leverage makes the post-bubble policy response, and the bond and gold payoff, much larger than in 2000.
insights.quote: you can expect a bigger recession and the Fed to react to that. So, so the the Fed, you know, maybe rates go back to zero whenever that happens

insights.claim: The market has swung from treating every shock as deflationary to treating every shock as inflationary and shunning bonds, but both shock types exist; the next deflationary shock (bubble burst, or AI-driven unemployment of 10%+) will make bonds work again.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Nominal bonds retain hedge value despite current hatred of them.

insights.claim: TIPS offer a higher Sharpe ratio than nominals for a buy-and-hold investor (even levered up), but they carry duration and are poor early in a hiking cycle; in stagflation they only work if the Fed does not hike, and the very short end holds up best.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Own TIPS strategically, but time duration exposure by the Fed cycle.

insights.claim: Bonds are increasingly hated, with more clients asking whether to own any at all, while gold and US equities are already heavily owned, so bonds look like the under-represented asset.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Crowded in gold and equities; bonds are the contrarian opposite once the hiking ends.

themes.theme: Dollar, Europe and the global equity map

insights.claim: Citi's four-factor EUR/USD model (relative equities, relative rates, terms of trade with an oil component, macro data momentum) is 3 to 1 in favor of the dollar, only data momentum favoring Europe, giving a dollar-bullish bias though the dollar is short-term oversold.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Dollar strength is tied to the AI equity trade, oil and relative rates; do not chase an oversold entry.

insights.claim: The ECB is closer to a policy mistake than the Fed: it is hiking on oil prices without an AI boom or second-round effects, and French spreads have already shown stress.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Euro-area rate and spread risk supports the dollar and argues for caution in European equities.

insights.claim: Citi is cautious on Europe (no AI exposure, hurt hardest by an energy shock, possible ECB overtightening, French election risk, weaker currency) though not outright bearish, since every market except China correlates strongly with the S&P.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Underweight Europe is a relative call, not a short; no market reliably moves opposite to the S&P.

insights.claim: Korea and Taiwan are essentially AI/DRAM plays, so to be consistent with a positive US AI view, emerging Asia belongs on the long side; Korea rose 80% in one quarter on levered retail then fell sharply, and Citi would prefer to buy once positioning cleans out more.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Asia tech offers no diversification from the US AI trade but is the consistent expression.

insights.claim: China equities have not tracked GDP or EPS growth, owing to hyper-competition and stakeholders other than shareholders capturing the gains, so impressive Chinese AI and products do not translate into an investable index thesis.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Avoid extrapolating China's industrial success into index returns; export strength with weak domestic demand is also drawing European pushback.

insights.claim: Global forces drive roughly 70% of emerging market returns, so when the global cycle turns, trade with the global cycle rather than the idiosyncratic story.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Idiosyncratic EM stories matter less than the S&P direction.

insights.claim: Citi likes Brazil because it is one of few idiosyncratic plays: a likely market-friendly new government, fiscal repair and aggressive rate cuts from real rates of 9 to 10%, in a commodity-linked market cheaper than its 15-year average.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Lower real rates plus a business-friendly regime support equities and the real, with carry cushioning the currency.

insights.claim: Brazilian equities have gone nowhere for about 18 years, leaving a burned and grim investor base; Meb argues a market flat for decades has stored mechanical potential to break out.
insights.speaker: Meb Faber
insights.so_what: Extreme pessimism after a long drought is a contrarian positive sign.

insights.claim: In Lula's first election in 2002 the real strengthened sharply once he moved to the center after weakening beforehand, and the S&P bottomed almost the same day, showing that markets are forward-looking and EM moves often follow global markets.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Pre-event risk premium means the opposite often happens after the event; check global drivers first.

insights.claim: Short-term gold trades off US real rates, which argue against buying now with a hawkish Fed, but the long-term bull case is central banks seeking non-dollar reserves, as Putin's diversification into euros, renminbi and gold left only gold viable.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Wait for the Fed hiking cycle to end before adding gold; structural central bank demand remains.

insights.claim: Citi's heuristic is that gold bottomed when the Bank of England finished selling and will peak when the PBOC finishes buying, and China could still buy a lot to cut dollar holdings.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: PBOC buying is the signal to monitor for a gold top.

insights.claim: Copper still works as a signal but via global data momentum rather than the copper/gold ratio; it has a higher Sharpe when data momentum rises, and does best with rising momentum plus a weak dollar, which is absent now, though AI and energy transition provide structural demand.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Copper is supported by strong data momentum but capped by a firmer dollar.

insights.claim: Credit is a cheap hedge against a bubble burst because spreads are already tight and supply is ample, so it underperforms in recession at little carry cost; hedging an Iran oil spike essentially requires buying expensive oil optionality because implied volatility is still high.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Underweighting credit is a low-cost hedge for the bubble scenario; oil hedges are costly.

themes.theme: 2027 outlook and the key macro question

insights.claim: Willer's base case is that the bubble keeps giving for another year, the Fed hiking cycle ends, the Iran situation resolves with oil back near $70 or lower (the war began amid an oil oversupply), allowing bonds to be added aggressively and central bank hiking cycles to turn to easing.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Next year likely favors adding duration and rotating within commodities as oil falls and rate pressure eases.

insights.claim: When oil falls and hiking ends, gold should make a comeback, creating a big rotation in commodities and bond behavior.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Gold's weakness tied to hawkish Fed repricing should reverse as the cycle ends.

insights.claim: The single biggest macro question is when the equity bubble peaks, since that triggers the Fed pivot, much lower rates, Fed purchases of the long end and a surge in gold; Citi devotes 80% of its effort to it though it is not the base case for next year.
insights.speaker: Dirk Willer
insights.so_what: Positioning for a bubble peak is the key asymmetric risk to monitor via the Generals and PULSE indicators.
